cases.vignette:
A 66-year-old female patient with a history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis and thrombocytopenia. The patient had consistently shown leukocytopenia and thrombocytopenia in routine blood tests over the years. Initial blood test revealed a leukocyte count of 3.16 × 10^9/L and a platelet count of 109.00 × 10^9/L. No other symptoms were present, and no significant abnormalities were detected in cardiac enzymes or blood coagulation. Four hours post-procedure, the patient experienced intermittent abdominal pain and occasional nausea. Nine hours following the operation, the patient experienced recurrent right abdomen pain progressing to involve the entire abdomen, with persistent nausea and perceived increase in body temperature.

Initial examination showed tenderness in the right abdomen, without rebound tenderness and muscular tension, with normal bowel sounds. Later examination revealed diffuse tenderness with rebound tenderness, primarily in the right abdomen. Dullness to percussion was observed, while pain during percussion in the liver area was absent. Shifting dullness to percussion was negative, and normal bowel sounds were detected. Maximum body temperature was 37.8°C.

- Laboratory Tests:

  - Absolute lymphocytes: 0.32 × 10^9/L
  - Platelet count: 79.00 × 10^9/L
  - CRP level: 2.45 mg/L
  - Procalcitonin level: 0.58 ng/ml

- Bacterial Culture:
  Ascites culture yielded growth of Escherichia coli.

A 56-year-old woman with locally advanced, unresectable pancreatic adenocarcinoma. She initially received four cycles of Folfirinox chemotherapy without significant response, followed by gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel therapy. He reported touching an unpasteurized sheep stomach with an injured hand about 1 month earlier. Initial outpatient therapy with oral cefprozil provided no lasting benefit. A 26-year-old woman presented with a 2-day history of burning on urination, urinary frequency, nocturia, and constant 5/10 suprapubic pain that did not radiate. She denied fever, nausea, vomiting, changes in bowel movements, weight change, palpitations, heat or cold intolerance, peripheral edema, and abnormal vaginal discharge. Her last menstrual period was one week earlier. Physical examination revealed lower abdominal tenderness, most pronounced in the para-umbilical area, without costovertebral angle tenderness.

Laboratory tests showed a negative serum β-hCG, normal CBC and BMP, and a urinalysis with 10–25 WBCs per high-power field, moderate bacteria, moderate mucus, moderate yeast, and positive nitrites; cervical NAAT was negative for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. A diagnosis of lower urinary tract infection was made, and she received a 10-day course of antibiotics as an outpatient.

Despite treatment, her dysuria, frequency, and burning worsened. She reported chronic constipation, with two hard, non-bloody stools per week managed intermittently with stool softeners. There was no history of abdominal trauma or family gastrointestinal disease. 

Because of persistent symptoms, a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis was performed. It demonstrated a 4.0 × 3.3 × 6.8 cm multiloculated, enhancing hypodense and isodense mass extending superiorly from the dome of the bladder to the posterior surface of the umbilicus, with surrounding acute inflammatory stranding and minimal fluid. There was possible invasion into the bladder dome, secondary thickening of an adjacent distal small-bowel loop, and perivesical stranding around a thick-walled, collapsed bladder.

Given these findings, differential diagnoses included patent urachus, urachal sinus, urachal diverticulum, and malignant transformation of a urachal remnant, and diagnostic laparoscopy was planned.

cases.vignette:
A 45-year-old man with a history of systemic lupus erythematosus, well controlled without immunomodulatory therapy, presented with a 30 × 20 mm painless, slowly progressive mass on his left forehead over 1 year. He had undergone excision of a similar frontal bone lesion diagnosed as fibrous dysplasia 2 years earlier. He denied headaches or neurologic symptoms.  
On CT scan, the lesion showed a ground-glass appearance with homogenous matrix expansion of the frontal bone, predominantly affecting the external cortex. Fine-needle aspiration cytology with immunostaining excluded multiple myeloma (no CD138+ cells). A core biopsy demonstrated diffuse sclerosis, complete bone resorption, and intra-trabecular fibrosis; the bone was not uniformly mineralized, and these findings were reported as suggestive of fibrous dysplasia.  
Preoperative laboratory tests, including inflammatory markers, renal function, and blood counts, were within normal limits. The patient underwent complete surgical excision of a 40 × 50 mm portion of frontal bone, including the lesion with a 15 mm margin of normal bone, via a coronal approach. The bone defect was repaired with an autologous calvarial graft using piezoelectric osteotomies.

cases.vignette:
A 51-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of gradually progressive pain and swelling below his left knee, accompanied by intermittent fevers. Three months before presentation, the swelling ulcerated. He remained ambulatory without assistance.  
On examination, there was a firm mass measuring 30 × 18 × 12 cm over the distal tibia extending into the calf, with an anterior discharging ulcer 12 cm in diameter and areas of necrosis. The discharge was yellow and thick. Knee range of motion was reduced, and there was tenderness over the left knee and proximal tibia. Distal pulses (dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial, popliteal) were intact and lower-limb neurologic examination was normal. Other systemic examination findings were unremarkable.  
Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. Chest radiograph showed no abnormalities. Plain radiographs of the left leg demonstrated a large metadiaphyseal lesion of the tibia with soft-tissue opacity, bone erosion and destruction of the tibia and adjacent fibula, and linear and ring-like calcifications, with extension into the proximal leg soft tissues. A Tc-99m bone scan revealed increased tracer uptake in the shaft of the left tibia and proximal soft tissue, without evidence of distant skeletal metastases. MRI was not obtained due to financial constraints.  
Based on the clinical presentation and radiographic appearance, the leading considerations were osteosarcoma and chondrosarcoma of the tibia. On admission, the patient received intravenous antibiotics and analgesics and was counseled regarding treatment options. Taking into account lesion size, secondary infection, prosthesis cost, and prognosis, the patient elected transfemoral amputation with plans for postoperative chemotherapy.

A 3-week-old male Sprague-Dawley rat was housed under standard conditions and assigned to a control group in a pharmacological study. At 7 weeks of age, the rat appeared clinically normal and was euthanized under anesthesia. At necropsy, the liver and other organs appeared grossly unremarkable, and serum AST and ALT levels were within normal limits.

A sample from the left lateral liver lobe was fixed in formalin, embedded, and stained with hematoxylin and eosin, Azan, and Watanabe’s silver stain. Histologically, there were multifocal basophilic foci located predominantly in the perilobular region. Within these foci, polygonal to short spindle-shaped cells formed small nests and sheets within dilated sinusoids without encapsulation. The tumor cells exhibited clear cell borders, high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios, hyperchromatic nuclei, frequent mitotic figures, and sparse hepatocellular necrosis. Narrow spaces containing erythrocytes were noted between tumor cells, and local invasion into adjacent blood vessels was seen. Azan and silver stains demonstrated reticular fibers forming a loosely connected, irregular network within tumor cell aggregates.

cases.vignette:
A 36-year-old G5P2+2 woman with two prior cesarean deliveries and two first-trimester miscarriages was referred at 6 weeks of amenorrhea for evaluation of a pregnancy of unknown location. Her serum quantitative β-hCG was 16,124 mIU/mL. A transabdominal ultrasound at presentation did not locate an intrauterine or extrauterine pregnancy. A copper intrauterine device had been removed 2 months before her last menstrual period. She had used one cycle of clomiphene. She had no chronic illnesses, did not smoke or drink, and was not on medications.

On examination, blood pressure was 113/70 mmHg, pulse 98 beats/min, and temperature 37.5 °C. Abdominal, cardiorespiratory, neurological, and pelvic examinations were unremarkable. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a 13 mm gestational sac with irregular margins and a yolk sac in the anterior isthmic portion of the uterus, raising suspicion for a cesarean-section scar ectopic pregnancy. Doppler was declined. Serial β-hCG measurements rose by 33% over 48 hours (21,521 mIU/mL). The patient missed follow-up and returned 1 week later with 5 days of worsening pelvic pain.

Repeat transvaginal scan revealed a fetal pole with cardiac activity (crown–rump length 0.9 cm) in a sac traversing the full width of the anterior myometrium, extending exophytically toward the serosa, with trophoblastic flow on Doppler; there was no endometrial fluid or free pelvic fluid. She was taken to laparoscopy and hysteroscopy: the bladder was densely adherent to the anterior uterine wall, the ectopic was not visualized, and extensive intrauterine adhesions obscured the view; there was no intracavitary bleeding. Postoperatively, she became hypotensive (systolic 82–95 mmHg) without vaginal bleeding. This prompted an urgent MRI to map the location of the pregnancy.

A 66-year-old man was referred for recurrent perianal abscesses over 12 months. His history included perianal trauma from sitting on broken glass in childhood; comorbidities were vascular dementia, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, atrial fibrillation, and gout. He reported no perianal warts, sexually transmitted diseases, immune deficiency, inflammatory dermatoses, arsenic exposure, or family history of malignancy. Examination revealed a fluctuant left lateral perianal mass without external fistulas. Ultrasound‐guided aspiration yielded 15 cc of purulent fluid; Gram stain and cultures were negative, but cytology showed atypical squamous cells. Postdrainage differential diagnosis included squamous cell carcinoma, cyst, condyloma, or large abscess. Two months later, the mass had enlarged, prompting concern for a fistula. Surgical drainage again yielded purulent fluid without microbial growth. On examination under anesthesia less than one month later, an external sinus tract into the mass was noted but no fistula to the anal canal. It was then decided to excise the mass completely and close the defect primarily.

cases.vignette:
A 65-year-old woman presented with a 5-month history of a slowly progressive orbital mass causing left exophthalmia, left hemifacial pain, and progressive visual impairment culminating in total vision loss.  
Her medical history included 8 years of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus, stage IIB cervical adenocarcinoma treated 3 years earlier with concurrent radiotherapy and weekly cisplatin, and well-controlled hypertension, dyslipidemia, and hypothyroidism.  
On examination, she had left exophthalmia with vision impairment and complete restriction of ocular motility. Anterior rhinoscopy, oral cavity, and neck examinations were unremarkable; nasofibrolaryngoscopy revealed a discrete medial bulging of the left nasal fossa lateral wall and a leftward septal deviation.  
Contrast-enhanced CT of the orbital region showed a soft-tissue density lesion occupying the left maxillary sinus with extension into the orbit, ethmoidal and sphenoid sinuses, and bone discontinuity of the maxillary, septal, sphenoid, ethmoidal walls, and pterygopalatine fossa. MRI demonstrated a heterogeneously enhancing mass in the left maxillary sinus, nasal cavity, ethmoidal sinuses, and intraorbital region, with bone disruption of the lateral and inferior orbital walls, extension through the inferior orbital fissure, invasion of the left cavernous sinus, diffusion restriction around the ophthalmic nerve, and anterior displacement of the extraocular muscles and vessels; these findings were considered highly suggestive of malignant neoplasm.  
Laboratory studies on admission showed HbA1c 8.8%, CRP 15.5 mg/L, ESR 120 mm/h, negative Cryptococcus antigen, nonreactive FTA-ABS, HIV, and hepatitis panels except positive anti-HBc, and CSF analysis with protein 58 mg/dL, glucose 66 mg/dL, WBC 5/mm3, IgG 11.3 mg/dL, negative cytology and cultures, and ADA 1.8 U/L.  
An endoscopic endonasal biopsy of the left maxillary sinus revealed on frozen section a probable low-grade lymphoproliferative lesion, but paraffin-fixed sections showed nonspecific chronic fibrosing inflammation without evidence of neoplasia, granulomas, or fungi.

cases.vignette:
A 19-month-old boy was brought to the emergency department after an episode of reduced consciousness while bathing. His parents reported that when lukewarm water was poured over his chest, he turned blue around the lips and began gasping for air. During this time, his eyes “rolled back,” and he did not interact with his parents. There were no clonic movements, and he did not respond to physical stimulation. He subsequently fell asleep for approximately 1 hour and was brought to the ED.

On arrival, he was alert and appeared well. There were no focal findings on examination, his development was appropriate, and laboratory studies—including a blood glucose level of 5.5 mmol/L—were normal. His parents reported similar, less profound episodes during bathing over the previous 2 weeks, in which his head would go back, his eyes would roll upward, and he would become floppy and limp for 2–3 minutes, followed by sleepiness. These episodes occurred only during bathing; contact with water in other settings did not provoke symptoms. He had normal developmental milestones and no significant past medical or family history.

An electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus rhythm with a normal QT interval. Bathing in lukewarm water while his vital signs were monitored provoked hypotonia, tachycardia, and brief apnea with associated desaturation. He stared straight ahead and made mouthing movements; he was removed from the bath, given high-flow oxygen, and again slept for about 1 hour. A further similar episode occurred later while he was sleeping, without any provocation. The first interictal EEG was normal using the standard 10–20 system. Because he was clinically well between episodes and there was an avoidable trigger, he was discharged with plans for follow-up investigations, including a brain MRI, a bathing EEG, and outpatient review.

cases.vignette:
A 9-year-old girl with a small muscular ventricular septal defect presented with chest pain and dyspnea one week after recovering from an upper respiratory infection and after minor anterior chest trauma in a fall. She was afebrile. Heart rate was 104 beats/min, respiratory rate 28 breaths/min, blood pressure 113/66 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation normal. Physical examination revealed mild tenderness over the sternum and normal cardiac auscultation. 

Chest radiography showed mild cardiomediastinal silhouette enlargement and a focal opacity in the right middle lung. ECG was normal. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a moderate circumferential pericardial effusion with right atrial collapse, normal biventricular systolic function, and no ventricular septal defect. 

Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 12,000 cells/µL with an absolute eosinophil count of 1,570 cells/µL (normal 40–190), C-reactive protein 1.94 mg/dL (normal <0.5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 45 mm/hr (normal 0–30), and troponin T 0.25 ng/mL (normal <0.1). Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed elevated global myocardial T2 (70 ms) and T1 (1150 ms) values, increased left ventricular wall thickness, a moderate pericardial effusion, and no late gadolinium enhancement.

She was admitted with a working diagnosis of viral myopericarditis. Treatment with oral ibuprofen and colchicine resulted in resolution of chest pain, normalization of troponin and inflammatory markers, and reduction of the pericardial effusion over three days. However, the absolute eosinophil count rose further. Consultations with infectious diseases, allergy/immunology, and rheumatology were obtained. Further history elicited pica and exposure to two dogs and a cat. 

Chest computed tomography revealed multiple pulmonary nodules with adjacent ground-glass opacities. An infectious workup showed negative PCR tests for influenza, respiratory syncytial virus, parainfluenza virus, rhinovirus, and adenovirus; negative Bartonella henselae titers; and a negative T-SPOT tuberculosis test. Mycoplasma pneumoniae IgM and IgG were elevated, but nasopharyngeal Mycoplasma PCR was negative. Toxocara serology was sent and was pending at discharge.

A 49-year-old woman was referred for surgical management of a presumed large nonfunctioning pituitary macroadenoma. She reported a 2-year history of chronic bitemporal headache, unexplained easy fatigability, and very slowly progressive diminution of vision. Her medical history was notable only for well-controlled hypertension. On examination, visual acuity was decreased bilaterally (worse on the left) with bitemporal homonymous hemianopia. Endocrinological evaluation revealed central hypothyroidism, and levothyroxine replacement was initiated. Noncontrast CT of the brain showed a slightly hyperdense large sellar/suprasellar mass extending into both cavernous sinuses with right parasellar extension and bony remodeling of the sella turcica and upper clivus. Contrast-enhanced MRI demonstrated a 36 × 41 × 50 mm sellar/suprasellar/parasellar mass with heterogeneous low T1 signal, intermediate high T2 signal, small central areas of diffusion restriction on DWI, and mild patchy postcontrast enhancement. The lesion encased the cavernous and clinoid segments of the right internal carotid artery and partially encased the left cavernous segment. The optic nerves and chiasm were elevated and inseparable from the mass, and the pituitary gland and stalk were not visualized.

cases.vignette:
A 71-year-old Hispanic man was referred for a 2-month history of dysphagia and left oropharyngeal fullness. His medical history included hypertension, dyslipidemia, atrial fibrillation, and a left superficial parotidectomy in 2008 for a Warthin tumor, followed by Frey syndrome. A 68-year-old woman presented with a 10-day history of hemoptysis and a 1-month history of mild cough, sputum production, and rhinorrhea. Her past medical history was unremarkable, with no malignancy, immunosuppressive therapy, diabetes mellitus, or vasculitis. On examination, vital signs were normal. Laboratory tests showed an elevated C-reactive protein level of 7 mg/dL (reference: 0–0.3 mg/dL) and a normal white-cell count with a neutrophil count of 3.97 × 10^3/μL. HIV testing was negative. Initial microbiologic studies—including bacterial cultures, acid-fast bacillus smear and culture of sputum, blood cultures (bacterial and fungal), and respiratory viral serologies—were all negative. 

A chest radiograph demonstrated multiple nodules and masses of various sizes in both lung fields, some with cavitation. Chest CT (lung window) showed cavitary and noncavitary nodules and masses with faint surrounding ground-glass opacity (“halo sign”). Cavitary lesions had thick, irregular walls with septa-like structures; on mediastinal windows, one lesion contained a hypoattenuating area. A coronal maximum intensity projection image showed patent vessels within the lesions. A small bilateral pleural effusion was present. 

Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody titers (both c-ANCA and p-ANCA) were within normal limits. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and transbronchial biopsy revealed diffuse granulomatous inflammation but no organisms. Video-assisted thoracoscopic wedge resection of a cavitary lesion was performed. Histopathologic analysis showed diffuse necrotizing granulomatous inflammation and fungal elements. Methenamine silver staining revealed yeast-like structures associated with septate hyphae demonstrating acute-angle branching.

cases.vignette:
A 12-year-old boy was referred for evaluation of a facial angioma. MRI of the brain showed no leptomeningeal vascular malformations. Examination revealed bilateral naevus flammeus along the ophthalmic and maxillary divisions of the trigeminal nerve, more extensive on the right. Visual acuity was 20/20 in each eye. Slit-lamp examination of the right eye showed iris heterochromia with diffuse hyperpigmentation and evenly distributed micronodular elevations on the iris surface. Intraocular pressure measured by Icare tonometry was 22 mm Hg in the right eye and 12 mm Hg in the left. Gonioscopy demonstrated open angles bilaterally with diffuse trabecular hyperpigmentation in the right eye. Anterior-segment OCT revealed increased reflectance of the iris surface in the right eye. Funduscopic examination showed increased retinal vessel tortuosity and a diffusely darker fundus in the right eye. B-scan ultrasonography measured choroidal thickness of 2.2 mm in the right eye versus 1.4 mm in the left. Macular spectral-domain OCT confirmed a thicker choroid in the right eye. Standard automated perimetry detected early visual-field defects in the right eye, and peripapillary OCT showed borderline retinal nerve-fibre-layer thickness on the right. Topical latanoprost was initiated in the right eye, reducing intraocular pressure to 17 mm Hg.

An 83-year-old man presented with 6 months of progressive right mandibular pain radiating to the zygomatic and mastoid regions, requiring oxycodone, paracetamol, and ketorolac for relief. An empirical course of prednisone (50 mg per day) for presumed trigeminal neuralgia provided no benefit. Contrast-enhanced maxillofacial CT showed enlargement of the right sphenoid sinus with overdevelopment and opacity of the lateral recess, bone thickening and sclerosis of the sphenoid walls, pterygoid process, and orbital apex, and focal interruption of the foramen rotundum and lateral recess wall. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI demonstrated soft tissue protruding through a breach in the lateral recess wall of the sphenoid sinus, invading the right internal pterygoid muscles, masticatory and pterygopalatine fossae, and infiltrating the V2 and V3 trigeminal branches; intracranial extension into the cavernous sinus surrounded the Gasserian ganglion, with the cavernous carotid artery patent. T2-weighted images showed a markedly hypointense signal in the lateral recess with peripheral mucosal inflammation. Endoscopic evaluation revealed purulent discharge in the sphenoethmoidal recess. The patient underwent right endoscopic sinus surgery: after middle turbinectomy, the sphenoid ostium was obstructed by a pyocele, which was marsupialized and drained; samples of the lesion and surrounding mucosa were sent for bacteriological and histopathological examination. The maxillary and ethmoid sinuses were then opened, the breach in the posterior-lateral sphenoid wall was repaired with mucoperiosteum, and a Merocel sponge was placed. He was discharged after 2 days without complications. Histopathology was negative for hyphae and neoplastic cells, and cultures grew no bacteria or fungi. One month after surgery, follow-up MRI confirmed persistent inflammation of the sphenoid sinus, skull base, and pterygoid fossa. A consultation with an infectious diseases specialist was sought.

Within 24 hours, massive hematuria recurred and her hemoglobin continued to fall despite further transfusion.

A 36-year-old man with end-stage renal disease secondary to IgA nephropathy underwent a live-related renal transplant 6 months ago and has been maintained on tacrolimus 3.5 mg daily, mycophenolate sodium 720 mg daily, and prednisolone 7.5 mg daily. He was afebrile on admission, heart rate 88 beats/min, blood pressure 122/76 mm Hg, respiratory rate 28 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Examination revealed bilateral inspiratory crackles; other findings were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL; total lymphocyte count 9900/μL; absolute neutrophil count 7720/μL; platelets 285 000/μL; serum creatinine 1.05 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas analysis demonstrated PaO₂ 68 mm Hg and an A–a gradient of 22 mm Hg. HIV ELISA was negative. Chest radiograph revealed bilateral diffuse alveolar infiltrates. High-resolution CT of the chest showed bilateral diffuse ground-glass opacities without pleural or mediastinal abnormalities.

Sputum induction was non-diagnostic. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid was positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii on Grocott’s methenamine silver stain and negative for acid-fast bacilli, CMV inclusion bodies, and fungal hyphae. He was treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and a prednisone taper, with clinical and radiographic resolution of infiltrates after 2 weeks.

A 15-year-old girl presented with multiple swellings of five months’ duration. She noted progressive enlargement of bilateral neck masses and one each on her back and anterior abdominal wall, without pain. There was no significant past medical, personal, or family history. 

On examination, there were seven subcutaneous, nontender, mobile swellings measuring 1×1 to 3×3 cm in the cervical regions, right paraspinal area, and anterior abdominal wall. The lesions were firm to hard without changes in the overlying skin. 

Complete blood count, metabolic panel, and skeletal survey were all normal. With a clinical impression of lymphoreticular malignancy or metastatic disease, fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) was performed on the most prominent swellings (two cervical, one paraspinal, one abdominal). 

Cytology smears from all sites showed moderate cellularity with similar features: predominantly plump spindle cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, fragments of collagenous matrix, and occasional small cells with scant cytoplasm. The spindle cells had bipolar cytoplasmic extensions and round-to-oval nuclei with fine granular chromatin; nucleoli were inconspicuous. Nuclear hyperchromasia, pleomorphism, or atypicality was not seen, and mitoses were sparse. There was no necrosis or inflammatory cells. 

Ultrasonography confirmed that all lesions were confined to the subcutaneous tissue, with no lymphadenopathy or deeper masses.

cases.vignette:
A 35-year-old man presented for routine follow‐up 11 years after a left total hip arthroplasty with a ceramic‐on‐ceramic articulation. Over the preceding 3 months, he had left buttock and greater trochanteric pain, initially attributed to overuse. He denied fevers or systemic symptoms. On examination, range of motion of the left hip was full and painless; there was focal tenderness over the posterior buttock and greater trochanter but no palpable mass. Anteroposterior radiographs of the pelvis and left hip were unchanged compared with images obtained 1 year earlier. A diagnosis of greater trochanteric bursitis was made, and an intra‐bursal corticosteroid injection was administered, resulting in partial symptom relief.

Six weeks later, he returned with persistent buttock pain and intermittent electric shock–like sensations radiating down the left leg. Physical examination now revealed decreased and painful range of motion of the left hip with continued tenderness over the greater trochanter. A lumbar spine radiograph was normal. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 22 mm/h (reference range, 2–28), a C‐reactive protein level of 14.4 mg/L (reference, <10.0), and an alkaline phosphatase level of 318 IU/L (reference, 40–125). Hip aspiration yielded 10,750 white cells/μL; all cultures were negative. Serum cobalt and chromium levels were within normal limits. A metal artifact reduction sequence MRI revealed a left periprosthetic soft‐tissue mass measuring 9 × 8 × 10 cm, without bony involvement or bone‐marrow edema.

Over two and a half years, he underwent extensive physiotherapy for presumed plantar fasciitis and tight gastrocnemius muscles, treatment with anti-inflammatory and analgesic medications, and two separate surgical releases (endoscopic plantar fascia release and minimally invasive gastrocnemius release) with only temporary relief. On re-presentation, he reported recurrent heel pain upon return to work.

On examination, he walked with an antalgic gait. The gastrocnemius remained tight with a positive Silfverskiöld test, and there was non-specific tenderness over the plantar aspect of the calcaneus at the insertion of the plantar fascia. 

Weight-bearing dorsoplantar and lateral radiographs of the foot demonstrated normal bony relationships with no fractures, lesions, or signs of arthritis. Magnetic resonance imaging of the left foot showed no thickening of the plantar fascia and no signal alteration in adjacent soft tissues or bone marrow. However, MRI revealed a pedunculated bony protrusion arising from the posterolateral plantar aspect of the calcaneus, measuring approximately 1.1 cm × 0.9 cm.

She reported progressively worsening sacral pain and local skin irritation but denied purulent discharge, altered bowel habits, rectal bleeding, or rectal discharge. Medications included aspirin, rosuvastatin, valsartan, and topical corticosteroids as needed.

On examination, she was afebrile and systemically well. The coccygectomy scar was slightly indurated and surrounded by a broad area of excoriated skin with plaques and focal ulceration in the upper natal cleft. A small superior sinus tract without obvious pits and mild serous discharge were noted. The lesion was located more than 5 cm from the anal verge. There was no exophytic mass, no underlying abscess cavity, and no palpable inguinal lymphadenopathy.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis with contrast demonstrated a 6 × 13 × 28 mm area of nonspecific, irregular superficial enhancement in the natal cleft without invasion of underlying structures, no visible sinus tract, and no regional nodal or bony metastases. A staging CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no metastatic disease.

cases.vignette:
A 19-year-old woman presented with an 18-month history of pain in the plantar aspect of her left foot.  The pain was moderate initially, often worse at night, and markedly exacerbated by compression and exposure to cold.  Over the past four months, the patient noted aggravation of the local pain and was referred for imaging.  She denied any trauma and had no family history of neurofibromatosis.  

On examination, three prominent, soft-tissue nodules with swelling and tenderness were palpated in the plantar aspect of the left foot; they were mobile and not adherent to surrounding tissue.  Sensation testing revealed numbness in the medial distal plantar foot; toe and foot motor strength were normal.  

Magnetic resonance imaging of the left foot demonstrated three nodules arranged in a linear distribution in the mid-plantar region.  On T1-weighted images, the lesions were homogeneously isointense to skeletal muscle.  On T2-weighted fat-suppressed images, they were homogeneously hyperintense without cystic degeneration; each was surrounded by a hyperintense rim.  A small extension of high signal from the lateral aspect of one lesion resembled a “mouse-tail.”  Two nodules were located within the flexor digitorum brevis muscle beneath the plantar aponeurosis, and one was in the superficial fascia at the third metatarsophalangeal joint.  The lesions followed the course of branches of the common plantar digital nerves without evidence of invasion.  

Based on the clinical presentation and imaging findings, the differential diagnosis included glomus tumor, neurofibroma, and schwannoma.  Multiple plexiform schwannoma was suspected, and surgical excision was recommended.

A 33-year-old man with a history of massive small-bowel and ileocecal resection 12 years earlier (leaving 40 cm of small intestine) was maintained on a normal diet after bowel rehabilitation. One month before admission, he developed diarrhea and a 7-kg weight loss with progressive weakness, anorexia, dizziness, and cachexia. On admission his weight was 36 kg (BMI 12.2 kg/m^2), heart rate 80 bpm, blood pressure 70/50 mmHg, and respiratory rate 18 bpm. He was alert and oriented. Physical examination showed pitting edema of the lower extremities, thin skin, a scaphoid abdomen, and no ascites. Chest radiography revealed a dense nodule outside the right upper lung field (thought to be rib calcification). Lower-limb radiographs and renal ultrasonography were normal; gallbladder ultrasonography showed atrophy. ECG demonstrated normal sinus rhythm with T-wave flattening/inversion in leads II, III, aVF, and V4–V6, and an incomplete right bundle-branch block. Initial laboratory values included: phosphate 1.10 mmol/L, potassium 3.1 mmol/L, sodium 144 mmol/L, glucose 6.0 mmol/L, magnesium 0.60 mmol/L, calcium 1.7 mmol/L, albumin 27.7 g/L, prealbumin 100 mg/dL, hemoglobin 48 g/L, hematocrit 14.0%, BUN 5.0 mmol/L, and creatinine 86 mg/dL. He was diagnosed with severe malnutrition and received blood transfusion; parenteral nutrition (500 kcal/day); fluids; electrolyte, trace-element, and multivitamin supplementation (including daily thiamine 100 mg IV). Over 24 hours his strength and edema improved. Then he acutely developed profound fatigue and flaccid weakness of all four limbs. cases.vignette:
A 35-year-old West African man with no prior psychiatric or medical history presented to clinic with a 1-week history of escalating behavioral changes. His family reported episodes of talkativeness, incoherent speech, visual and auditory hallucinations, insomnia, and grandiose and persecutory delusions. He denied head injury, substance use, or stressors and had no family history of psychiatric illness. He worked as a mechanical engineer in a mining community with potential mercury exposure and had no systemic or respiratory symptoms despite known community spread of COVID-19.

On examination he was afebrile, BP 135/80 mmHg, pulse 88 bpm, and with normal respiratory rate and oxygen saturation. General and neurologic exams were unremarkable. He appeared disheveled, restless, and agitated but was oriented to time, place, and person. Speech was loud and clear without latency. He exhibited circumstantial thought, grandiose delusions (“I am a prophet of God”), persecutory delusions, and both auditory (“gunshots”) and visual (a mob) hallucinations. Memory was intact and he had no insight.

Laboratory studies showed a normal CBC, renal function, and albumin; γ‐glutamyl transferase was elevated at 81 IU/L (normal < 55) and total bilirubin 26 μmol/L (normal 3.4–20.5). Malaria and typhoid screens were negative. Urinalysis revealed transient proteinuria and glycosuria that normalized on repeat. Head CT scan was normal. A lateral flow COVID-19 antigen test and confirmatory RT-PCR were both positive.

MR is a male neonate born at 38 weeks’ gestation by elective cesarean delivery. Birth weight was 2350 g (5th–10th percentile), length 45 cm (5th percentile), head circumference 31 cm (<5th percentile). Apgar scores were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes.  
Maternal history was notable only for immunity to rubella, negative toxoplasma serology, and a single CMV serology at 11 weeks (IgG positive, IgM negative). A maternal febrile episode occurred in the periconceptional period; there was no trauma, and no use of cocaine, warfarin, or anticonvulsants. No family history of bleeding disorders or stroke.  
Fetal ultrasound at 20 weeks suggested intracranial hemorrhage, confirmed by fetal MRI at 25 weeks, which showed a 2.3 cm porencephalic cyst in the right frontotemporal–insular region with ex vacuo enlargement of the right lateral ventricle, reduced right cerebral hemisphere volume, and abnormal micropolygyria of the right frontal cortex.  
At birth, examination revealed microcephaly, jaundice, micropurpura on the face and upper thorax, mild upper limb hypertonicity, and abnormal deep tendon reflexes. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, coagulation profile, assays of clotting factors (II, V, VII, IX, X, XI, XIII), protein C and S, von Willebrand factor, alpha-2 antiplasmin, antithrombin, APC resistance, lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and beta-2 glycoprotein antibodies, were all normal. Gene sequencing for MTHFR and factor V Leiden was wild type. Newborn metabolic screening was negative.  
Cranial ultrasound on day 1 showed a right porencephalic area with “ex vacuo” enlargement of the right lateral ventricle and a germinolytic cyst on the left; MRI confirmed these findings, with no vascular malformations or thrombosis.

cases.vignette:
An 18-year-old man presented with 6 months of fluctuating lower-limb weakness. He awoke one morning unable to move his legs but recovered movement over 30 minutes, with residual unsteadiness. He remained asymptomatic for 4 months, then developed ascending spastic weakness of the lower limbs over 3 months until he was unable to stand, accompanied by urinary retention requiring a Foley catheter and one month of constipation. He denied trauma, fever, steroid or other drug intake, and infections.

On examination he was non-obese (65 kg, 167 cm; BMI 23.3 kg/m2) with no signs of Cushing syndrome or endocrinopathy. Neurologic examination showed increased tone and preserved bulk in the lower limbs, Medical Research Council grade 3/5 at hips and knees and 0/5 at ankles and toes, brisk knee and ankle jerks, bilateral extensor plantar responses, and graded sensory loss below the D10 level. The spine was neither deformed nor tender. Routine hematological and biochemical tests and cerebrospinal fluid analysis were normal. Plain radiographs of the spine were unremarkable.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the thoracic spine demonstrated a posterior epidural mass from D5 to D7, with a maximum thickness of 10 mm that was homogeneously hyperintense on both T1-weighted and T2-weighted sequences, suggestive of fat.

cases.vignette:
A 41-year-old woman with a 3-year history of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis presented with the sudden onset of visual disturbances. At the time of her SSc diagnosis, she had skin sclerosis of the fingers, hands, forearms, and face, Raynaud’s phenomenon with digital ulcers, multiple facial telangiectasias, esophageal reflux, and interstitial lung disease. Nail-fold capillaroscopy showed capillary loss with dilatation and microhemorrhages. A forearm skin biopsy demonstrated increased dermal collagen and superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltration. Laboratory studies revealed a positive antinuclear antibody titer (>1:320) with a nucleolar pattern, negative anti-centromere antibody, and negative anti-Scl-70 antibody. She was treated with bosentan and aspirin, with stable pulmonary findings over two years.

Seven days before transfer, she was admitted elsewhere for fever over 38°C and headache. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed protein 161.6 mg/dL, glucose 39 mg/dL, red blood cells 0 /mm3, and white blood cells 459 /mm3 (88% polymorphonuclear cells). Serum C-reactive protein was 10.6 mg/dL and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 82 mm/h. Brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated T2 hyperintense lesions in the frontal, left parietal, and left occipital lobes with leptomeningeal enhancement. Empirical ceftriaxone and vancomycin were initiated. After four days, she developed visual disturbances; repeat MRI showed increased size and number of multifocal T2 hyperintense lesions along both cerebral hemispheres and midbrain, including a 4.5-cm lesion in the right posterior lobe. Tests of CSF—including Gram stain and culture, PCR for herpes simplex virus and enteroviruses, cryptococcal antigen, and fungal cultures—were negative. She was then referred to our hospital.

On arrival, she could only count fingers at close range and also reported headache, dizziness, fever, myalgia, polyarthralgia, and bilateral foot tingling. Blood pressure was 192/103 mmHg, heart rate 48 beats/min, and temperature 37.3°C. Electrocardiogram showed sinus bradycardia. Neurologic examination revealed drowsiness, neck stiffness, symmetrical proximal and distal weakness (muscle strength 4/5), paresthesia in both feet, brisk biceps reflexes, absent patellar reflexes, and bilaterally positive Babinski signs. A 4 × 5 cm ulcer was noted over the right lateral malleolus; there was no synovitis. The white-cell count was 14,090 /mm3, C-reactive protein was 3.09 mg/dL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 56 mm/h. She continued antibiotics, and intravenous acyclovir, nicardipine, mannitol, and dexamethasone were added. Blood pressure stabilized within six hours, but her visual impairment worsened, and she developed left-sided weakness and new Raynaud’s phenomenon in her fingers. Emergent cerebral angiography revealed diffuse stenosis and a beaded pattern of the anterior and middle cerebral arteries and their branches, along with diffuse luminal narrowing and dysplastic changes in the right distal vertebral artery and basilar trunk, consistent with cerebral angiitis.

A 37-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, was found on routine blood screening at 10 weeks’ gestation to have pancytopenia: platelet count 85×10^9/L, white-cell count 2.3×10^9/L (neutrophils 1.3×10^9/L, monocytes 0.2×10^9/L), and hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL. Her only prior pregnancy, 13 months earlier, was uncomplicated with normal platelet counts. She had equivocal hypothyroidism, a family history of thyroid disease and systemic lupus erythematosus, and no new medications. Thyroid function, immunoglobulins, folate, and vitamin B12 were normal; antinuclear antibody was negative. Ferritin was low, and iron supplements were started.

She was given a presumptive diagnosis of immune thrombocytopenia in pregnancy. Her fatigue persisted but she had no bleeding complications. At 38 weeks’ gestation, with a platelet count of 61×10^9/L, prednisolone 20 mg daily was initiated without response (platelets 65×10^9/L), followed by intravenous immunoglobulin at 1 g/kg (platelets 52×10^9/L). She underwent spontaneous vaginal delivery at 38 weeks with minor bleeding; her platelet count was 52×10^9/L, and the neonate’s platelet count was normal.

Five weeks postpartum, she developed a pustular rash on the left upper arm, abdomen, and back. Skin biopsy showed dermal neutrophils with upper dermal edema and a subepidermal blister, consistent with bullous Sweet’s syndrome. Her blood counts remained low: hemoglobin 13.0 g/dL, white-cell count 1.7×10^9/L (neutrophils 0.5×10^9/L, monocytes 0.1×10^9/L), and platelets 49×10^9/L.

A 52-year-old Chinese man presented with bilateral red eyes and itching for 1 year. The redness was constant with intermittent tearing, without pain, gritty sensation, photophobia, or discharge. He reported episodic blurred vision due to dry eye, relieved by lubricants. He denied diplopia. His medical history included type 2 diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia (all treated), and a chronic maculopapular rash on the chest and arms suggestive of atopy or eczema. He had no sinusitis, asthma, other autoimmune or dermatologic disorders, drug allergies, prior immunosuppression, ocular trauma or surgery, contact-lens wear, or family history of ocular or skin disease. He did not smoke.

On examination, vital signs were normal. He had a maculopapular rash over flexor and extensor surfaces of his elbows without excoriations. There were no rosacea-type or acneform facial lesions and no oral ulcers. Ocular examination showed bilateral moderate diffuse bulbar conjunctival hyperemia and grade 1 subtarsal papillary reaction. Each eye had an inferior symblepharon involving up to three clock hours and cicatrization of the caruncle. The inferior lacrimal punctum was scarred. There was no chemosis, scleral nodules, or ankyloblepharon.

Fluorescein staining revealed faint inferior punctate corneal staining in both eyes without epithelial defects, filaments, infiltrates, or edema. There were superficial inferonasal corneal scars in the right eye without thinning or vascularization. Corneal sensation was normal. Tear-breakup times were 4 seconds (right) and 5 seconds (left), and Schirmer I test values were 20 mm and 25 mm at 5 minutes, respectively. A few misdirected lower-eyelid lashes did not touch the cornea. Marx’s line showed mild advancement in the upper lids and borderline changes in the lower lids. Meibomian gland evaluation revealed no liquid meibum; manual expression yielded minimal viscous secretion from a single gland. Uncorrected visual acuity was 6/7.5 in each eye. Intraocular pressures were 17 mmHg (right) and 19 mmHg (left). Anterior chambers were deep and quiet, and the vitreous and posterior segments were unremarkable.

A clinical diagnosis of chronic cicatricial conjunctivitis was made.

A 53-year-old man was admitted for progressive dyspnea (NYHA class III). His history included a congenital ventricular septal defect repaired in childhood, subsequent aortic valve and septal patch replacements, permanent atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, chronic hepatitis C–related liver disease, and prior admission for heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. On examination, he had jugular venous distension, irregular rhythm, a 2/6 systolic murmur at the aortic and mitral areas, decreased breath sounds at the right lung base, and peripheral edema.  
ECG showed atrial fibrillation with left bundle branch block. Chest radiography demonstrated pulmonary congestion and a right basal pleural effusion. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed: a dilated left ventricle with preserved ejection fraction (60%), a dilated right ventricle with normal systolic function, no residual septal shunt, a normally functioning mechanical aortic prosthesis but elevated transprosthetic gradients (mean 33 mmHg) with an effective orifice area index of 0.4 cm2/m2 (suggesting severe prosthesis–patient mismatch), moderate mitral regurgitation, severe tricuspid regurgitation, and estimated systolic pulmonary artery pressure of 50 mmHg. The inferior vena cava was dilated with poor inspiratory collapse.  
An initial diagnosis of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction was made, and intravenous diuretics led to reduction of edema and resolution of radiographic congestion, but the patient remained dyspneic with low exercise tolerance and still required supplemental oxygen.  
A contrast CT scan of the chest and abdomen showed a small right pleural effusion, no lung parenchymal disease or pulmonary embolism, cirrhotic liver with a focal lesion suspicious for hepatocellular carcinoma, splenomegaly, and signs of portal hypertension.  
Right heart catheterization revealed a high cardiac output state, normal pulmonary vascular resistance, and only a slight elevation of mean pulmonary and wedge pressures.
